passage:
October. Parul skipped her Kathak class again to sit with Harish in the canteen. "You don't mind, na?" she asked. He shrugged. She told her friend Anu she'd come for Sunday lunch "next time."
December. Anu's messages sat unread. Parul realised she had laughed at Harish's jokes all month but couldn't remember her own last idea. In her hostel room the ankle bells hung dusty on a nail. She felt small, and oddly lonely beside someone she loved.
February. "Tuesdays and Thursdays are dance," Parul told Harish. "Sunday I'm with Anu." He frowned, then asked, "Fine. When's the recital?" That evening she practised until her feet ached, and for the first time in months she called him with news of her own.

qa.q: What hung dusty on a nail in Parul's hostel room in December?
qa.a: Her ankle bells.

qa.q: What was Parul feeling in December when she couldn't remember her own last idea?
qa.a: She felt small and oddly lonely, even beside someone she loved, as if she had lost part of herself.

qa.q: What choice in February changed things, and why did it help?
qa.a: Parul told Harish her dance days and her Sunday with Anu. Keeping her own time gave her news of her own to share, so she was close without disappearing.

qa.q: How might Harish see Parul's new schedule?
qa.a: At first he seems unsettled, since he frowns, but then he asks about her recital, so he may come to enjoy a partner with her own life.

grounding: A young woman in her first serious relationship drops her dance and friends, then reclaims them and finds closeness works better with her self intact.

passage: Sit, Dhruv. You asked why I look worried when you vanish with your girlfriend for weeks. Let me tell you about your Chacha, Manoj, at twenty. I did the opposite. I loved a girl in my B.Com class, Kiran, but I kept her at arm's length. I never told her Baba's shop was failing, never let her meet my friends, never let her see me upset. I thought a wall kept me safe. Once she said, "I feel like I'm dating your good side." She left after a year. Years later, with your Chachi, I tried something new. I showed her the messy parts, and I still kept my Sunday chess with my friends. Close, but still me. So don't vanish, and don't hide. Both cost me something.

qa.q: What did Kiran once say to Manoj?
qa.a: "I feel like I'm dating your good side."

qa.q: Why did Manoj keep Kiran at arm's length?
qa.a: He thought a wall kept him safe, so he was afraid of getting hurt if she saw troubles like Baba's failing shop.

qa.q: What did Manoj do differently with Chachi, and why did it work better?
qa.a: He showed her the messy parts while still keeping Sunday chess with his friends, so he was both close and still himself.

qa.q: How might Kiran have felt in that relationship?
qa.a: She probably felt shut out and lonely, as if she only knew a polished version of him, which is why she left.

grounding: An uncle recalls keeping a partner at arm's length and later learning to be close while keeping his own friends and self.

passage: It was the week before semester exams, the hostel team's final was on Saturday, and Leena had asked Hrithik to help at her cousin's engagement that same evening. For two months he had said yes to everything she wanted. He had skipped practice four times, and Pankaj, his oldest friend, had stopped saving him a seat at dinner. Sitting on the hostel stairs with twelve percent battery, Hrithik typed "Of course I'll come" and stopped. He thought of Pankaj's face at the last match. He deleted it and wrote, "I'm playing the final at five, it matters to me. I'll come straight after, maybe by eight." The reply took ages. "Okay. A bit sad, but okay." Then he messaged Pankaj: "Still need a striker?"

qa.q: How many times had Hrithik skipped practice?
qa.a: Four times.

qa.q: How was Hrithik feeling when he deleted "Of course I'll come"?
qa.a: He felt uneasy about how far he'd drifted from Pankaj and his team, and realised the final mattered to him too.

qa.q: What made Hrithik's reply to Leena a balanced choice?
qa.a: He kept his commitment to the team and still offered to come afterwards, staying close to Leena without giving up something that matters to him.

qa.q: How might Pankaj feel on getting "Still need a striker?"
qa.a: Pankaj may feel glad to have an old friend back, though perhaps a little wary after two months of empty seats 🙂

grounding: A young man who has dropped his friends and sport for a new relationship chooses to stay close to his partner while keeping his own life.

passage:
Rekha had been with Charu for eight months, and his friends at their Chennai college had still never met her. She kept him in neat compartments: Tuesday dinners, Saturday walks along the beach road, nothing else. When he invited her to his sister's birthday, she said she had a class.
Then her internship interview went badly, and she sat alone on the hostel stairs for an hour instead of calling him. He found out from her roommate. On the phone that night his voice was quiet. "I don't know if I know you, Rekha. You tell me about films, never about you."
She almost said she was fine. Instead she said, "I thought if you saw me upset, you'd leave." A long silence. "I'm still here," he said.
She went to the birthday the next Sunday. She also kept her Friday painting class, just for her.

qa.q: What reason did Rekha give for not going to his sister's birthday?
qa.a: She said she had a class.

qa.q: Why did Rekha keep Charu in neat compartments?
qa.a: She was afraid that if he saw her upset he would leave, so keeping him at a distance felt safer.

qa.q: What was the turning point, and what did Rekha choose?
qa.a: When Charu said he didn't know her; instead of saying she was fine, she told him her fear, which let them actually get closer.

qa.q: How did it feel for Charu to hear about the bad interview from Rekha's roommate?
qa.a: He likely felt hurt and shut out, wondering whether he really knew the person he had been with for eight months.

grounding: A young woman keeps her first serious partner at arm's length to stay safe, then risks being known while keeping her own painting class.

passage:
"You've missed badminton three Thursdays," Joseph said, stirring his tea in the canteen. "Your captain asked if I'd kidnapped you."
Anjali laughed. "I'd rather be here with you."
"You were here with me yesterday. And Monday. And you skipped Swapna's birthday."
"You didn't mind."
"I didn't. But I'm starting to." He set the cup down. "When I met you, you talked nonstop about smashes and your hostel gang. Now you only talk about us."
Anjali looked at her hands. "If I'm not around, I worry you'll get bored of me."
"I'm more likely to get bored of me," Joseph said. "Go to practice. Tell me who you beat."
"And you?"
"I have my drawing class. We'll eat together after."
Anjali took out her phone and messaged the captain: back on Thursday.

qa.q: How many Thursdays of badminton had Anjali missed?
qa.a: She had missed three Thursdays.

qa.q: What is Anjali worried about when she stays with Joseph all the time?
qa.a: She worries that if she's not around, he will get bored of her.

qa.q: What choice at the end helps Anjali stay close to Joseph and still be herself?
qa.a: She messages the captain that she's back on Thursday, keeping her badminton and friends while still eating with Joseph after.

qa.q: Why might Joseph say he is 'starting to' mind?
qa.a: He misses the lively person he met, who had her own game and friends, and worries she is losing herself in the relationship.

grounding: A young woman who dropped her sport and friends to be close to her partner is nudged back toward keeping a self while staying close.

passage:
Dear Anjali,
It's been almost a year, and I'm sorry it took me this long to write.
When I started seeing Rohit, I let everything else slide. I skipped our Sunday badminton, then stopped replying to the group, then missed your birthday dinner because he wanted a quiet evening. I told myself that's what being close meant: always there, always yes.
Last month he asked what I wanted for my birthday and I couldn't answer. I didn't know what I even liked anymore. That scared me more than any fight.
I'm not leaving him. I love him. But I've signed up for badminton again, Saturdays, and I've told him that's my morning.
I miss you. I miss who I was with you. Would you play a match with me, if you still want to?
Love,
Charu

qa.q: Which day is Charu's new badminton?
qa.a: Charu has signed up for badminton on Saturdays.

qa.q: Why did Charu feel scared when Rohit asked about her birthday?
qa.a: Charu was frightened to realise that nothing felt like a clear personal wish anymore, which showed how much of Charu's own self had disappeared into the relationship.

qa.q: What is Charu's letter doing well as a repair?
qa.a: It owns the specific ways Charu let Anjali down, gives a concrete step, and invites Anjali back without pressure, so Anjali can choose.

qa.q: How might Anjali feel reading this letter after almost a year?
qa.a: Anjali may feel a mix of hurt from being dropped and warmth at being missed, and could need time before saying yes to a match.

grounding: A young adult in a first serious relationship notices having dropped friends and interests to be close, and starts reclaiming a self that can stay whole.

passage: So you want to know why Sunaina almost left? Honestly, it was me. I'm Sarika, I'm twenty-one, and when we started dating I kept everything on a timer. Two dinners a week, never at my flat, never with my friends. She'd ask about my family and I'd change the topic. I told myself I was keeping my independence. Really I was scared that if she saw all of me, she'd go, and I'd be the one left standing. Then one night she said, very quietly, "I feel like I'm dating your calendar." That hit. I didn't fix it overnight. I brought her to my friend's birthday. I told her about my parents' divorce, badly, crying into a plate of momos. I still keep my Friday evenings for painting. But now she knows what's in the paintings.

qa.q: What did Sunaina say that hit Sarika?
qa.a: Sunaina said, "I feel like I'm dating your calendar."

qa.q: What was Sarika really afraid of when keeping Sunaina at a distance?
qa.a: Sarika was afraid Sunaina would leave after seeing everything, so the distance was protection against being hurt, not true independence.

qa.q: Which of Sarika's changes shows a healthy balance, and why?
qa.a: Keeping Friday painting while sharing its meaning with Sunaina shows Sarika can stay herself and still let Sunaina close.

qa.q: How might the arm's-length rules have felt for Sunaina?
qa.a: Sunaina probably felt shut out and lonely inside the relationship, as if she was scheduled rather than wanted.

grounding: A young adult in a first serious relationship keeps a partner at arm's length for safety and learns that closeness needs a self that can open while staying whole.

passage:
Week one: Mehak cancels her Thursday pottery class because Kishore finishes work early on Thursdays. "It's just one class," she tells her flatmate, and spends the evening watching him play video games.
Week five: The unfinished bowl sits dusty on her shelf. Her college friends have made a group plan without asking her. Mehak scrolls through their photos at midnight, a little hollow, wondering when she last did anything that was only hers.
Week eight: She's back at the wheel, clay up to her wrists. Kishore picks her up after class and asks to see the new mug. On the drive home she tells him she also wants one weekend a month with her friends. He's quiet, then says, "Okay. I didn't realise you'd stopped." Mehak squeezes his hand, relieved and still hers.

qa.q: Why did Mehak cancel her Thursday pottery class in week one?
qa.a: She cancelled it because Kishore finishes work early on Thursdays.

qa.q: What was Mehak feeling when she scrolled her friends' photos at midnight?
qa.a: Mehak felt hollow and left out, sensing that she had lost the things that were only hers.

qa.q: What could Mehak's week-eight choices teach someone in a first serious relationship?
qa.a: Staying close does not mean giving up everything; returning to pottery and asking for time with friends kept the relationship and her self both alive.

qa.q: How does Kishore seem to see Mehak's changes?
qa.a: Kishore seems surprised, since he hadn't noticed she had stopped, but he accepts her request and shows interest in her new mug.

grounding: Across weeks, a young adult first drops a hobby and friends to be close to her partner, then rebuilds a self that stays whole while staying close.

passage:
"Farhan, you're spending every minute with your girlfriend, I see. Let your Dadu tell you something.
At twenty, I, Siddharth, fell in love with a girl in my college in Lucknow. I stopped playing hockey. I stopped meeting my friends. I even stopped painting, which I loved. I thought love meant being together every second.
After six months, she said, 'I don't know who you are any more. You just agree with me.'
It hurt. But she was right. I'd melted into her.
So I went back to hockey on Sundays. I painted again. My friends forgave me. And strangely, we grew closer when I had a self to bring back to her.
Love needs two whole people, beta. Not one and a half."

qa.q: What did Siddharth stop doing when he fell in love?
qa.a: He stopped playing hockey, meeting his friends and painting.

qa.q: How did young Siddharth feel when she said she didn't know who he was?
qa.a: He felt hurt, but also realised she was right that he had lost himself.

qa.q: What was the turning point in the story, and what did it lead to?
qa.a: Her words; Siddharth went back to hockey, painting and friends, and they grew closer.

qa.q: How might the girlfriend have felt when he just agreed with everything?
qa.a: She probably felt lonely and confused, missing the real person she had fallen for.

grounding: An elder recalls dropping friends and interests to merge with a first love, and learning that intimacy needs a self that stays whole.

passage:
Jaya had one week before her final exams, and her boyfriend of four months was texting her every hour, asking why she wasn't free. She had already stopped going to her dance class and skipped her friend Payal's birthday to spend time with him.
Now, sitting in the library with a pile of notes, her phone buzzed again: "Why aren't you answering? 😢"
Jaya looked at the message and felt a strange tightness. She realised she hadn't talked to Payal properly in weeks. She didn't even know what she liked any more, except him.
She typed: "I love you. But I need to study this week. And I miss my friends."
She put the phone face down and texted Payal separately: "Sorry about your birthday. Can we have chai on Sunday?"
Payal replied at once: "Yes! Missed you."

qa.q: Whose birthday had Jaya skipped?
qa.a: She had skipped her friend Payal's birthday.

qa.q: What was Jaya feeling as she looked at her boyfriend's message?
qa.a: She felt a strange tightness, uneasy at realising she had lost her friends and interests in the relationship.

qa.q: Which of Jaya's steps help her keep a self in the relationship?
qa.a: Telling her boyfriend she needs to study and misses her friends, and reaching out to Payal for chai.

qa.q: How might Payal feel receiving Jaya's text?
qa.a: Payal feels happy and relieved, saying she missed Jaya.

grounding: A young woman who dropped friends and interests for a first relationship notices she is losing herself and starts to reclaim her whole self.

passage:
Francis and Seema had been dating for a year in Bengaluru. Seema often asked, "Why don't you ever talk about your family? Your worries?"
Francis would shrug. "Nothing to tell." He kept his weekends for his cycling group and his evenings for himself. He liked Seema a lot. But getting close felt risky, like handing someone a map to hurt him.
One evening Seema said quietly, "I feel like I'm dating a locked door."
That night Francis lay awake. He realised he'd kept everyone at arm's length since his parents' divorce. Safe, but lonely.
The next evening he called her. "Can I tell you about my father?" His voice shook. Seema listened for an hour.
He didn't stop cycling. But he started letting her in.

qa.q: What did Francis keep his weekends for?
qa.a: He kept his weekends for his cycling group.

qa.q: What was Francis feeling when he lay awake that night?
qa.a: He felt lonely and uneasy, realising he'd kept everyone at arm's length since his parents' divorce to stay safe.

qa.q: How did Francis begin to find a balance between closeness and self?
qa.a: He kept his cycling but began sharing his inner life with Seema, starting with the call about his father.

qa.q: How did Seema feel before Francis opened up?
qa.a: Seema felt shut out and lonely, as if dating a locked door.

grounding: A young adult keeps his partner at arm's length to stay safe, and learns that intimacy needs a whole self that also lets someone in.

passage:
'You skipped dance again?' Eshaan asked, when Damini turned up at his hostel gate at six.
'I'd rather be with you.'
'That's three weeks. And you didn't go to Ritika's birthday.'
'Ritika will survive.'
'Damini, I like you. A lot. But I also liked the girl who argued about Kathak with me for an hour on our first date.'
She laughed, then stopped. 'When we're apart I keep thinking you'll get bored and leave.'
'So you're giving up everything so I don't?'
'Sounds bad when you say it.'
'Go to class tomorrow. Then come and tell me what your teacher yelled at you about.'
'And Ritika?'
'Call her tonight. I'll be here Saturday. I'm not going anywhere.'

qa.q: How long had Damini been skipping dance?
qa.a: Three weeks.

qa.q: What is Damini afraid of when apart from Eshaan?
qa.a: Damini is anxious that Eshaan will get bored and leave, which is why she drops dance and friends to stay close.

qa.q: What could help Damini stay close without losing herself?
qa.a: Keeping dance and friends like Ritika in her week, and talking to Eshaan about the fear instead of acting on it.

qa.q: How does Eshaan feel about Damini dropping everything?
qa.a: Eshaan is fond but uneasy; he misses the Damini who argued about Kathak and wants her whole self in the relationship.

grounding: A young woman in her first serious relationship drops friends and dance to stay close, and her partner urges her to stay whole.

passage: I'm Sarita, and for the first four months with Mehak I kept a door half-closed. We met in the college theatre club, and I liked her more than I'd ever liked anyone. That's exactly why I was careful. I never told her about my parents' divorce, never let her see me cry, cancelled plans when I felt too much. I thought I was protecting myself. She thought I didn't care. One night she said, 'I feel like I'm dating a very polite stranger.' That line stayed with me. Slowly, I tried: one real thing a week. The first was tiny, that I hate my own laugh. Later, bigger things. I still keep my own friends and my Sunday runs; I'm not disappearing into her. But the door is open now, and nothing terrible came through it.

qa.q: Where did Sarita and Mehak meet?
qa.a: In the college theatre club.

qa.q: Why did Sarita keep a door half-closed at first?
qa.a: Sarita felt afraid of being hurt precisely because the feelings were so strong, so staying guarded felt safer.

qa.q: What approach helped Sarita open up without losing a sense of self?
qa.a: Sharing one real thing a week while keeping friends and Sunday runs, so closeness grew at a safe pace.

qa.q: What was it like for Mehak before Sarita opened up?
qa.a: Mehak felt shut out and unsure she was cared for, like dating a very polite stranger.

grounding: A young adult looks back on keeping a first partner at arm's length and learning to open up while keeping a whole self.

passage:
Student counselling note, third year, week 6.
Pooja came in saying she felt 'hollow'. Over the session it emerged that since she began dating Jatin in August, she has stopped attending the debate society she founded, moved her study hours to match his and no longer sees her roommates on weekends. She said, 'He never asked me to. I just want to be where he is.' She also said, quietly, that she can't remember what she likes any more. Nothing she described suggested pressure or control from Jatin. I reflected back that closeness is good, and that a relationship needs two whole people. We agreed on one small experiment: attend next Thursday's debate meeting and have dinner with her roommates once. Follow-up booked for week 8.

qa.q: What society had Pooja founded?
qa.a: The debate society.

qa.q: What does Pooja mean by feeling 'hollow'?
qa.a: Pooja feels empty and lost, having dropped her own interests and friends so completely that she can't remember what she likes.

qa.q: Why is a small experiment better than telling Pooja to step back from Jatin?
qa.a: It helps her reclaim parts of herself gradually without making the relationship the problem, so she can stay close and whole.

qa.q: How might Pooja's roommates have experienced these weeks?
qa.a: Her roommates may have felt dropped and a little hurt, missing her on weekends without knowing why.

grounding: A counsellor's note shows a young woman merging into her first serious relationship and taking a small step to keep her own self.

passage:
Eid, 11 pm.
Diary, I have to be honest tonight.
Lakshmi came over with sheer khurma and asked why I've skipped dance practice three Sundays running.
I said Farhan and I had plans. True.
But also the art club. And our Thursday chai.
I've been folding myself into his timetable like a paper napkin, and I called it love.
This evening, watching Lakshmi laugh with my cousins, I missed the old Noor, the one who danced badly and loudly.
The strange part: I thought pulling back from everyone would make us closer.
It just made me smaller.
Tomorrow I'm going to practice.
I'll tell Farhan why, kindly, over the phone.
If being close means disappearing, it isn't the closeness I want.

qa.q: What did Lakshmi bring when coming over?
qa.a: Sheer khurma.

qa.q: What does Noor worry about by the end of the entry?
qa.a: Noor feels uneasy and wistful, missing the loud, dancing self and worried that folding into Farhan's timetable has meant disappearing.

qa.q: What would you advise Noor to say to Farhan?
qa.a: To explain calmly that Noor still wants the relationship but also needs Sunday dance and time with friends, so both of them can stay whole while being close.

qa.q: How might Lakshmi have felt about the missed Sundays?
qa.a: Lakshmi may have felt left out and a bit worried, which is why the question came with a bowl of sheer khurma rather than blame.

grounding: A young adult in a first serious relationship notices friends and interests slipping away and decides to keep a self while staying close.
